extracted.intended_audience: data visualization designers, analysts, journalists, and anyone creating charts
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Edward Tufte's principles to create truthful, clear, and informative data visualizations that prioritize information over decoration. Guidance covers comparison, causality, multivariate display, documentation, labeling, and avoiding misleading or decorative elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show Data in Comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated number is meaningless. Authority and insight come from context - showing how one value relates to others. The fundamental analytical question is always: 'Compared to what?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons reveal differences, trends, and anomalies that single data points cannot show. Use juxtaposition across time periods, regions, or categories. Weak example: isolated data (a single number provides no context). Strong example: multiple data points revealing steady growth over 3 years. Ensure comparisons are fair (see Lie Factor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lie Factor / Fair Comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Lie Factor = (Size of effect in graphic) / (Size of effect in data). A Lie Factor of 1.0 indicates an honest graphic. Values between 0.95 and 1.05 are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify how much a graphic deviates from numerical reality. Common sources of high Lie Factors: using area to represent one-dimensional data (squared effect), truncating the y-axis, applying perspective distortion. Case studies: fuel-economy chart (Lie Factor 14.8× due to perspective) and broken y-axis example (Lie Factor 36×). Avoid these manipulations to keep visual change proportional to data change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximize Data-Ink Ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Data-Ink Ratio = Data-Ink / Total Ink Used. 'Above all else, show the data.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to maximize the proportion of ink that represents data by erasing non-data-ink (borders, backgrounds, unnecessary gridlines) and redundant data-ink (duplicate labels). While a ratio of 1.0 is ideal and rarely achievable, designers should remove elements that don't convey information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate Causality (Reveal Mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts should suggest mechanism — they help viewers understand why something happened, not just that it happened. Effective graphics should reveal causality, mechanism, explanation, and systematic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotate events, align multiple variables to show cause-and-effect, and use visual sequencing (e.g., waterfall charts) to show how you got from Point A to Point B. Case study: Minard's map integrates army size, geographic path, temperature timeline, and direction to make causation (winter as the killer) visually evident. Avoid presenting correlations without context or causal markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show Multivariate Data
rubrics_metrics.description: The real world is complex. Oversimplified single-variable charts can mislead. Authoritative visualizations embrace complexity by showing how multiple variables interact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer encodings that combine time, value, region, category, etc., in a single view where appropriate. Weak example: single-variable bar chart that misses relationships. Strong example: a view encoding time, revenue, region, and units sold to reveal patterns impossible to see in isolation. Use precise registration so variables align meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate Evidence (Text, Numbers, and Graphics Together)
rubrics_metrics.description: Text, numbers, and graphics should work together seamlessly. The viewer shouldn't have to shuttle between a legend, a chart, and a separate text block to understand the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct labeling (integrated labels) instead of separate legend boxes which force eye movement and break cognitive flow. Integrate annotations, data values, and explanatory text directly in or adjacent to the graphic to minimize cognitive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document Everything (Attribution and Caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every chart should clearly state its source, the time period covered, and any important caveats about the data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include complete attribution with sources, dates, and methodology to build trust and enable verification. Weak example: unattributed data which lacks credibility. Strong example: full documentation that allows readers to verify claims and understand measurement context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content Above All / Avoid Chartjunk
rubrics_metrics.description: The design must serve the content, not the designer. 'Chartjunk' — decorative elements that add no informational value — undermines authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 3D effects, shadows, gradients, decorative backgrounds, excessive gridlines, and redundant encoding (e.g., using both color and pattern to express the same variable). Recognize 'The Duck' anti-pattern where visual metaphor overwhelms the data. Ensure every visual element serves an informational purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Distorting Scales and Perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use perspective distortion, inappropriate area encodings, or truncated axes that exaggerate or misrepresent differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: perspective distortion that exaggerated fuel economy improvements; broken y-axis that made a 5.6% data change look like 200% visual change. Avoid encoding one-dimensional data with area or 3D perspective; don't truncate baselines unless clearly justified and documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Labeling Over Segregated Legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct labeling creates immediate understanding. Separate legend boxes force viewers' eyes to jump between data and labels, breaking the flow of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place labels directly on chart elements when possible so viewers don't have to match colors/patterns to a legend. This integration reduces cognitive effort and improves clarity, especially in multi-series or multivariate displays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Simplicity — Remove Anything That Doesn't Add Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Could I remove any element without losing information? The goal isn't minimalism for its own sake. It's clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before publishing, check: Is the data shown in meaningful comparison? Does the design help explain why, not just what? Have I shown relevant complexity? Are labels integrated? Is the source documented? Remove elements (gridlines, borders, decoration, redundant encodings) that don't improve understanding.
